# The Jevons paradox of decisions {#sec-ch19}

```{python}
#| include: false
from jevkit import econ
```

In 1865 a 29-year-old economist named William Stanley Jevons published a book about coal, and it made him famous almost overnight [@jevons1865].

Britain ran on coal. Its factories, mines, ships and railways all burned it, and people had started to worry about how long it would last. The comforting answer was engineering. James Watt's steam engine got far more work out of each ton than the engines before it, and engineers kept improving it. Surely, as engines got more efficient, Britain would need less coal.

Jevons said no. More efficient engines had made coal-powered work *cheaper*, and cheaper work got used for more things. Engines that had been too costly to run became worth running, in more mills and more mines. Each engine used less coal. Britain used far more.

::: {.bookquote by="William Stanley Jevons, The Coal Question, 1865"}
It is wholly a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to a diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth.
:::

A model whose name is short for Jevons [[VERIFY]] invites the question: what's the coal, this time?

It's decisions.

![The pattern Jevons saw in coal, and the same pattern with decisions. Making each unit cheaper opens up uses that weren't worth it before, and total use can rise.](/figures/ch19/loop.pdf){#fig-loop}

::: {.goals}
- Explain the Jevons paradox with everyday examples, and say when it happens and when it doesn't.
- Work out when a decision is worth making at all, from its value, its price and its deadline.
- Model how many decisions a company makes as the price per decision falls, and what it spends.
- See where the paradox really bites: in new uses, not old ones.
- Spot the catch: cheap decisions move the load onto the people who review them.
:::

## Cheaper things get used for more things

You already know this pattern, even if you've never heard Jevons' name.

Think about photographs. When a photo meant film, developing and a trip to the chemist, you took a few dozen on a holiday and chose each one with care. Then each photo became essentially free. Nobody takes the same few dozen photos for less money. You take thousands, of receipts and parking spots and whiteboards, because each one is now worth taking.

Or light. Over the last two centuries, the price of an hour of light fell enormously, from candles to gas to electric bulbs to LEDs. Economic historians who traced it for the UK found that people didn't pocket the savings and keep a candle's worth of light. They lit streets and buildings and kept them lit all night, and use grew far faster than the price fell [@fouquet2006] [[VERIFY]].

That pattern has a name. The **Jevons paradox** is what happens when something becomes more efficient to use, each unit of use gets cheaper, and total use rises instead of falling.

## When it happens, and when it doesn't

The paradox isn't a law. Plenty of things got cheaper without anyone using much more of them. Salt is cheap, and you don't eat ten times as much as your great-grandparents did.

What decides it is how hungry people are for more, which economists measure as **elasticity**: how much the amount people use changes when the price changes. Total spend is price times quantity, so there are three cases.

![Three ways demand can respond to a falling price (illustrative). If people use only a little more when it's cheaper, total spend falls. If use grows exactly as fast as the price falls, spend stays flat. If use grows faster, spend rises: that's the Jevons paradox.](/figures/ch19/elasticity.pdf){#fig-elasticity}

If demand is **inelastic**, like salt, a price cut mostly saves money. If demand is **elastic**, like photos or light, a price cut opens up so many new uses that the total bill goes *up* (@fig-elasticity). Economists call the general effect a rebound, and they reserve "backfire" for the case where it more than cancels the saving. How often full backfire happens with energy is still argued over [@sorrell2009] [[VERIFY]].

So the question for decisions isn't "is the paradox true?" It's: *how elastic is the demand for decisions?* Are there lots of decisions that aren't being made today, only because they cost too much?

## Why a model would be named after it

TypeSafe has said the name nods to Jevons: that cheaper intelligence leads to wider use, not less of it [[VERIFY]]. It's a good choice, and a pointed one, because the same idea did the rounds in early 2025, when cheaper AI models briefly rattled investors and several technology leaders reached for Jevons to argue that cheaper AI would mean more AI, not less [[VERIFY]].

[[AUTHOR STORY: a decision you once wanted a system to make on every item, but couldn't justify the cost or wait, e.g. in AttendX or SIGNAL]]

We don't need to settle that argument for the whole industry. We can look at one company and count.

## The decisions nobody makes

Every decision has a **value**: the expected loss it avoids. Chapter 5 gave you the tools to put a number on it. Checking an alert that has a 3% chance of being a \$10,000 breach, when a good decision would stop it, is worth about \$300. A decision is worth making when its value is above its price.

Here's the thing about Kestrel. Its SOC makes a few thousand careful decisions a day. But the company generates millions of *possible* decisions: every inbound email, every login, every line in the logs. Each is almost certainly fine. Each is worth checking for a sliver of a cent.

I've built a small, deliberately simple model of this, and I want to be clear about what it is. Every number in it is an assumption, chosen to be plausible and written down in `jevkit/econ.py` where you can change it. It isn't a measurement of Kestrel or anyone else.

::: {.tryit lab="ch19"}
```{python}
for p in econ.POOLS:
    print(f"{p.name:>21}: {p.per_day:>9,} a day, "
          f"typical value ${p.median_value:.5f}".rstrip("0").rstrip("."))
```
:::

![Kestrel's decision pools (illustrative). Each line spans the middle 90% of decision values in a pool, with the median as a dot. A decision is worth making when its value is to the right of its price. At the LLM price, most emails, logins and log lines aren't worth asking about. At Jev's vendor-reported price, most are.](/figures/ch19/pools.pdf){#fig-pools}

Look at the long bottom rows of @fig-pools. There are {{< num ch19 pool_raw int >}} log events a day. A typical one is worth about two thousandths of a cent to check. At the book's illustrative LLM price of \${{< num ch19 llm_price f5 >}} a decision, only a sliver of them clear the bar. At Jev's vendor-reported price of \${{< num ch19 jev_price f6 >}}, about half of them do.

## Two gates, not one

Price isn't the only thing that stops a decision being made. Time does too.

When someone logs in, they're sitting there waiting. You might have a few hundred milliseconds to decide whether the login looks risky before the delay becomes the problem. An email can wait a few seconds before it's delivered. An alert can wait a minute.

![A decision gets made only if it's cheap enough (value above price) and fast enough (answer inside the time budget). The shaded regions show which decisions each option can make, using this book's illustrative LLM figures and Jev's vendor-reported price and latency range. Logins fall inside Jev's region only at the fast end of that range.](/figures/ch19/gates.pdf){#fig-gates}

@fig-gates puts both gates on one chart. The LLM's region starts at over a second and at a price that rules out the cheap pools. Jev's region reaches much further left, and further down. Logins are the interesting case: they fall inside Jev's region only if its calls land at the fast end of the vendor's range. That's a thing you'd measure before promising anyone real-time login checks.

## Kestrel's day, counted

Now we can count a whole day. Start from the price: as it falls, how many decisions are worth making, and what does Kestrel spend?

![Decisions worth making per day, and total spend, as the price per decision falls (illustrative; price gate only). Decisions climb steeply. Spend falls, because the newly affordable decisions are each worth so little.](/figures/ch19/curve.pdf){#fig-curve}

With both gates applied, the illustrative LLM makes {{< num ch19 llm_decisions int >}} decisions a day and spends about \${{< num ch19 llm_spend int >}}. Jev, at the fast end of its range, makes {{< num ch19 jev_decisions int >}} and spends about \${{< num ch19 jev_spend int >}}. That's about {{< num ch19 decisions_ratio int >}} times as many decisions for a quarter of the bill.

Notice what didn't happen. The bill went *down*. Inside Kestrel's existing jobs, demand for decisions is elastic enough to multiply the count, but not elastic enough to raise the spend. The newly affordable decisions are worth so little each that they add only about \${{< num ch19 value_gain int >}} a day of avoided loss.

*"So where's the paradox?"*

It's in the jobs that don't exist yet.

Suppose cheap decisions let Kestrel build something new: checking every file that's shared outside the company, {{< num ch19 new_job int >}} a day, each worth about three thousandths of a cent. At LLM prices almost nobody would build that. At Jev's price, the model takes {{< num ch19 jev_new_taken int >}} of those checks a day, and Kestrel's decision bill jumps from \${{< num ch19 jev_spend int >}} to about \${{< num ch19 jev_new_spend int >}}.

::: {.keyidea}
Cheaper decisions rarely raise the bill for the jobs you already do. They raise it by making new jobs worth doing.
:::

Add two or three more jobs like that and Kestrel spends more on decisions than it ever did with an LLM, while making dozens of times as many. That's Jevons' coal, in miniature. It's also what TypeSafe's Doom demo from Chapter 16 was really showing: an agent making ten decisions a second is a use that simply didn't exist when each decision took a second and cost a tenth of a cent.

## The catch: where the load goes

There's a second, less comfortable consequence, and it's the one I'd want you to remember on a Monday morning.

More decisions means more *outcomes* that someone has to deal with. Some of those million decisions will say "this looks bad", and a person will be asked to look.

![Alerts sent to a person per day, under two rules (illustrative). A rule that flags a fixed share of what the model looks at scales with the number of decisions, and swamps the team's capacity at Jev volumes. A cost line, which flags only when the expected loss is larger than the cost of a review, barely moves.](/figures/ch19/flags.pdf){#fig-flags}

Suppose you carried over a rule that seemed sensible at LLM volumes: send the top 0.1% of what the model looks at to a person. That sends {{< num ch19 flags_top_llm int >}} a day, comfortably under the team's capacity of {{< num ch19 capacity int >}}. At Jev volumes, the same rule sends {{< num ch19 flags_top_jev int >}} (@fig-flags). Nobody changed the policy. The queue just grew eightfold.

The cost line from Chapter 5 doesn't have this problem. It flags a case when its expected loss is bigger than the \$15 a review costs, and a log line worth two thousandths of a cent is never going to clear that. It sends {{< num ch19 flags_cost_jev int >}} a day either way.

::: {.keyidea}
When decisions get cheap, thresholds must be set by cost, not by share. Otherwise the saving on machines turns into a bill for people.
:::

That's also why calibration matters more, not less, as decisions multiply. A cost line only works if the probabilities are honest. An overconfident model making a million decisions a day doesn't make a few extra mistakes. It fills the queue.

::: {.breaks}
Everything in this chapter's Kestrel model is an assumption: the pools, their sizes, the value of each decision, the time budgets. Change them and the numbers move a lot, which is exactly why the lab lets you. Jev's price and latency are vendor-reported, and early-access prices can change. The "value of a decision" is itself an estimate that depends on calibrated probabilities, which Chapter 18 showed you can't assume. And historical analogies are suggestive, not proof: whether demand for decisions turns out more like light or more like salt is something only the next few years will show.
:::

::: {.threshold}
Kestrel wants to check every login in real time. There are 150,000 a day; a typical check is worth about \$0.0005; the budget is 300 milliseconds. At Jev's vendor-reported price, is the check worth making? What would you need to measure before switching it on? And what should the rule be for sending a login to a person?

(At \$0.000021 a check, yes: a typical login is worth about twenty times the price of checking it. The open question is time, so measure Jev's latency from your own network at your own volumes, including the slow tail. Send a login to a person only when its expected loss exceeds the cost of a review, never as a fixed share.)
:::

## Where we are

Jevons noticed that better engines made coal-powered work cheaper, and cheaper work spread until Britain burned more coal than ever. Decisions, we found, work the same way, with a twist. Inside the jobs a company already does, cheaper decisions multiply the count and shrink the bill. The paradox arrives through new jobs, ones that were never worth doing at a tenth of a cent. And every extra decision can turn into work for a person, unless the lines are drawn by cost.

Part IV has been about Jev on its own: what it is, what it answers, whether its probabilities can be trusted and what it might do to demand. Part V puts it in context, against every other way of making the same decision.

2. In the lab, halve the value of every raw log event. How many fewer decisions does Jev make? Does the bill change much? Why not?
3. Add a new job of your own design to the model. What value per decision and daily volume does it need before Kestrel's Jev bill doubles?
4. The "top 0.1%" rule sounded sensible. Write down a rule from your own work that is set as a share, not a cost. What would happen to it if volume went up tenfold?
